both can follow one DUI.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-R04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Does the DMV wait for the court to decide a DUI case before taking its own action?","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},"answer":{"text":"No; the DMV's administrative action stands regardless of the court's findings.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04"]},"rationale":{"text":"An administrative penalty is the DMV's action and stands regardless of the court's findings, while a criminal penalty is imposed by the court.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Driving under the influence","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"How alcohol and drugs impair.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F04"]},{"text":"Marijuana limits.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F04"]},{"text":"Two kinds of penalties.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson opens the chapter on driving under the influence. Alcohol slows brain function, affects how you process information and delays hand-eye coordination, and driving above the zero point zero eight legal limit raises crash risk from five times to as much as thirty times. Drugs can impair driving too. We will cover the marijuana limits, the crash figures the handbook reports, and the two kinds of DUI penalties in Nevada, administrative and criminal, which can both follow from a single arrest and run on their own separate tracks.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Alcohol and drugs","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alcohol slows thinking and coordination.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},{"text":"Medical and illegal drugs both impair.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},{"text":"Do not drive under their influence.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Alcohol slows brain function, affects how you process information and delays hand-eye coordination, and driving above the zero point zero eight legal limit raises crash risk from five times to as much as thirty times. Both medical drugs and illegal or prescription-controlled drugs can seriously harm motor skills and the ability to think and react, so do not drive under their influence. A prescription does not make a drug safe to drive on. If a medicine affects your thinking or reactions, the handbook's advice is simply not to drive while it does.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Marijuana limits","fact_ids":["sec12-F03","sec12-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Legal to use, limited for driving.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03","sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Two nanograms per milliliter of blood.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03","sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Five nanograms of metabolite.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03","sec12-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Although marijuana is legal in Nevada, it is unlawful to drive or be in actual physical control of a vehicle with more than two nanograms of marijuana per milliliter of blood, or five nanograms of marijuana metabolite. So the law separates using marijuana from driving with it in your system. Being in actual physical control of a vehicle counts too, not only driving it down the road. Under the Illegal Per Se Law, any detectable amount of a controlled substance can also revoke your driving privilege, which is covered in the next lesson.","fact_ids":["sec12-F03","sec12-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The crash figures","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-R12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Over thirty-one percent of deaths in twenty sixteen.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-R12"]},{"text":"Thousands of injury crashes.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-R12"]},{"text":"Forty-two percent in twenty nineteen.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-R12"]}],"narration":{"text":"The handbook reports that in twenty sixteen alcohol-related crashes were a factor in over thirty-one percent of Nevada roadway deaths, and that from twenty twelve to twenty fifteen alcohol and drugs contributed to four thousand six hundred fifty-one injury crashes in the state. It also notes that in twenty nineteen, one hundred twenty-nine people died in alcohol-related crashes in Nevada, forty-two percent of all traffic deaths. Alcohol and drugs together contributed to thousands of injury crashes in just four years.","fact_ids":["sec12-R03","sec12-R12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":32,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two separate tracks","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Administrative: the DMV.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},{"text":"Criminal: the courts.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},{"text":"DMV action stands regardless.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many people think a DUI case is decided only in court, so a not-guilty verdict would end everything. Nevada DUI law has two kinds of penalties: administrative action by the DMV, taken regardless of what the court finds, and criminal action by the courts. An administrative penalty is the DMV's action and stands regardless of the court's findings, while a criminal penalty is imposed by the court. So a driver can lose the license through the DMV even while the court case is still open or ends differently.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the DMV's role","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"A DUI court case is pending.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},{"text":"Does the DMV wait?","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver's DUI case is still pending in court. Does the DMV wait for the court before taking its own action? Decide before reading on. No. The DMV's administrative action is taken regardless of what the court finds. Nevada DUI law has two separate kinds of penalties, administrative action by the DMV and criminal action by the courts, and the administrative one stands on its own. That is why a driver can face a license revocation from the DMV and separate criminal penalties from the court for the same DUI.","fact_ids":["sec12-R04","sec12-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"DUI basics recap","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-R03","sec12-R12","sec12-F04","sec12-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alcohol and drugs both impair.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-R03","sec12-R12","sec12-F04","sec12-R04"]},{"text":"Marijuana has blood limits.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-R03","sec12-R12","sec12-F04","sec12-R04"]},{"text":"DMV and court penalties.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-R03","sec12-R12","sec12-F04","sec12-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To review, alcohol slows brain function, processing and coordination, and driving above the zero point zero eight limit raises crash risk from five to as much as thirty times. Medical and illegal drugs can both impair driving. Marijuana is legal, but driving with more than two nanograms per milliliter of blood, or five nanograms of metabolite, is not. Alcohol was a factor in over thirty-one percent of Nevada road deaths in twenty sixteen and forty-two percent in twenty nineteen. DUI brings DMV administrative action regardless of the court, plus criminal penalties from the court.","fact_ids":["sec12-F01","sec12-F02","sec12-F03","sec12-R03","sec12-R12","sec12-F04","sec12-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec12-u02","module_id":"sec12-m02","objective_ids":["sec12-u02"],"title":{"text":"Testing and per se limits","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Driving in Nevada means agreeing to chemical testing when an officer suspects DUI.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06"]},{"text":"The per se limits differ by driver, and drivers under twenty-one face a much lower one.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07","sec12-F08","sec12-F12"]},{"text":"Any license loss can be challenged by requesting an administrative hearing through the DMV.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A driver stopped on suspicion of DUI refuses the breath test for the first time ever.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F05"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Refusing the officer-directed tests revokes your driving privilege, with no eligibility for one year on a first refusal.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-R01"]},"result":{"text":"The driver's privilege is revoked, and the driver cannot be licensed for one year; an officer may also order a blood draw.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F05"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a driver below zero point zero eight percent cannot be convicted of DUI.","fact_ids":["sec12-F09"]},"correction":{"text":"The zero point zero eight percent level is only a guide, and you can be arrested and convicted of DUI at a lower alcohol concentration.","fact_ids":["sec12-F09","sec12-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Zero eight adults, zero four commercial, zero two under twenty-one.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F12"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"After losing a license, what can a driver request through the DMV?","fact_ids":["sec12-F10"]},"answer":{"text":"An administrative hearing.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10"]},"rationale":{"text":"Whenever you lose your license, you can request an administrative hearing through the DMV.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Tests and limits","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F07","sec12-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Implied consent.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F07","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"Per se limits.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F07","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"Hearings.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F07","sec12-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers chemical testing and the legal alcohol limits. Under the Implied Consent Law, a driver an officer suspects of DUI will be asked to take a blood, breath or urine test, and refusing has its own penalty. Under the Illegal Per Se Law, certain test results revoke your driving privilege by themselves. We will look at the limits for adults, drivers under twenty-one and commercial drivers, why you can be convicted below the limit, and the administrative hearing you may request whenever you lose your license.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F07","sec12-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Implied consent","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Blood, breath or urine tests.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06"]},{"text":"Blood draws even on a first offense.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06"]},{"text":"Refusal revokes the privilege.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Under the Implied Consent Law, a driver an officer suspects of DUI will be asked to take a blood, breath or urine test, and an officer may order a blood draw even on a first offense. Refusing the officer-directed tests revokes your driving privilege, with no eligibility for one year on a first refusal, or three years if your privilege was revoked for refusal in the prior seven years. So refusing a test is not a way to avoid consequences; the refusal itself brings a revocation, and a repeat refusal brings a much longer one.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Per se limits","fact_ids":["sec12-F07","sec12-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Adults: zero point zero eight percent.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07","sec12-F08"]},{"text":"Any detectable controlled substance.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07","sec12-F08"]},{"text":"Under twenty-one: zero point zero two.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07","sec12-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Under the Illegal Per Se Law, a chemical test showing zero point zero eight percent alcohol concentration or more, or any detectable amount of a controlled substance, revokes your driving privilege. A driver under twenty-one whose test shows an alcohol concentration of zero point zero two percent or more but under zero point zero eight percent loses the driving privilege administratively, and the officer can take the license on the spot. So the young driver's line is far lower than the adult line, and any detectable controlled substance counts for every driver.","fact_ids":["sec12-F07","sec12-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Commercial drivers and lower levels","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Commercial per se level: zero point zero four.","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"Any alcohol can affect a CDL.","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"The limit is only a guide.","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"For a commercial driver license holder, the administrative per se level starts at zero point zero four percent alcohol concentration. For commercial license holders, any detectable alcohol can affect the driving privilege, and DUI penalties are harsher, including lifetime disqualification from commercial driving. The zero point zero eight percent level is only a guide, and you can be arrested and convicted of DUI at a lower alcohol concentration. Whenever you lose your license, you can request an administrative hearing through the DMV.","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":33,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Refusal or result?","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Implied consent: refusing a test.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Per se: the test result.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Both revoke the privilege.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Implied consent and illegal per se are two different laws that both lead to revocation. Implied consent is about refusing a test, which brings revocation for refusal. Illegal per se is about the test result itself, which brings revocation at zero point zero eight percent or with any detectable controlled substance. When a question describes a driver who would not take the test, think implied consent and the one-year or three-year ineligibility. When it describes a test result, think per se and the alcohol levels.","fact_ids":["sec12-R01","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Three alcohol levels","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-F08","sec12-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Adults: zero point zero eight.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-F08","sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Commercial: zero point zero four.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-F08","sec12-F07"]},{"text":"Under twenty-one: zero point zero two.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-F08","sec12-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"The adult per se level is zero point zero eight percent alcohol concentration, while drivers under twenty-one face action starting at zero point zero two percent. For commercial license holders, the administrative per se level starts at zero point zero four percent. So there are three numbers to keep straight, and they belong to three kinds of drivers: the general adult driver, the commercial driver, and the driver under twenty-one. A test result that is legal for one of them can cost another the privilege, which is why the driver's status matters as much as the number.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-F08","sec12-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the hearing right","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"A driver loses the license.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},{"text":"What can they request?","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: after losing a license, what can a driver request through the DMV? Recall the rule before reading on. An administrative hearing. The handbook says that whenever you lose your license, you can request an administrative hearing through the DMV. That applies whether the loss came from refusing a test under implied consent or from a per se test result. It is part of the administrative side of DUI law, which runs separately from any criminal case in court. The hearing is requested through the DMV, not the court.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F06","sec12-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Testing recap","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-R01","sec12-F08","sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Refusal revokes.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-R01","sec12-F08","sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"Per se results revoke.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-R01","sec12-F08","sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]},{"text":"Three alcohol levels.","fact_ids":["sec12-F05","sec12-F06","sec12-F07","sec12-R01","sec12-F08","sec12-R02","sec12-F12","sec12-R08","sec12-F09","sec12-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, a driver suspected of DUI will be asked to take a blood, breath or urine test, and an officer may order a blood draw even on a first offense. Refusing revokes the privilege, with one year of ineligibility on a first refusal or three years after a prior refusal revocation within seven years. A test at zero point zero eight percent or more, or any detectable controlled substance, revokes the privilege. Drivers under twenty-one face action from zero point zero two percent and commercial drivers from zero point zero four. You can be convicted below the limit, and you may request a offense.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F14","sec12-F19"]},{"text":"Ignition interlock.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F14","sec12-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers DUI penalties. On the administrative side, an illegal per se action for zero point zero eight percent or a detectable controlled substance revokes the driver license for one hundred eighty-five days, may require an SR-twenty-two, and may be followed by criminal penalties. On the criminal side, penalties rise with each offense: first, second within seven years, third or later, and DUI causing death or serious injury. We will go up that ladder step by step and finish with the ignition interlock, which can restore driving privileges immediately.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F14","sec12-F19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Administrative revocations","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Per se: one hundred eighty-five days.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F13"]},{"text":"Under twenty-one: the same period.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F13"]},{"text":"SR-twenty-two may be required.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"An administrative illegal per se action for zero point zero eight percent or a detectable controlled substance revokes the driver license for one hundred eighty-five days, may require an SR-twenty-two, and may be followed by criminal penalties. On the penalty page, drivers under twenty-one at zero point zero two percent alcohol concentration also have the license revoked for one hundred eighty-five days, may need an SR-twenty-two, and may face criminal penalties. So the administrative revocation is the same length for adults over the adult limit and for young drivers over the youth limit.","fact_ids":["sec12-F11","sec12-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"A first DUI","fact_ids":["sec12-F14","sec12-F15","sec12-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"At least one hundred eighty-five days revoked.","fact_ids":["sec12-F14","sec12-F15","sec12-R09"]},{"text":"Jail or community service.","fact_ids":["sec12-F14","sec12-F15","sec12-R09"]},{"text":"Four hundred to one thousand dollars.","fact_ids":["sec12-F14","sec12-F15","sec12-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"A first DUI conviction brings license revocation for at least one hundred eighty-five days, two days to six months in jail or forty-eight to ninety-six hours of community service, and a fine of four hundred to one thousand dollars.
